summary.title: Reduced residence time of droplet impact on heated surfaces
summary.authors: Song Rong, Shiquan Shen, Tianyou Wang, and Zhizhao Che
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the impact dynamics of droplets on heated surfaces, specifically focusing on reducing the residence time of the impact process. The authors identify a new droplet bouncing mode, termed the 'bouncing-with-spray' (BWS) mode, which significantly reduces residence time compared to the traditional 'retraction-bouncing' (RB) mode. The BWS mode is induced by the burst of vapor bubbles within the liquid film, which creates holes in the film and causes the liquid to recoil from these holes, thereby shortening the recoiling distance and time. The study demonstrates that this heat-induced approach is simple, reliable, and avoids the surface degradation associated with microstructured surfaces. Experimental results show that the residence time in the BWS mode is independent of liquid viscosity. A theoretical model is proposed based on energy balance and a critical condition where the vapor bubble radius equals the minimum film thickness. This model yields a scaling law for the transition boundary between RB and BWS modes in the film boiling regime, expressed as ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ for constant liquid and droplet size. The scaling law agrees well with experimental data and also explains the transition behavior in the transition boiling regime. The findings provide physical insight into impact dynamics and offer a practical method for optimizing processes requiring rapid droplet departure, such as anti-icing and self-cleaning.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the impact dynamics of droplets on heated surfaces, specifically focusing on reducing the residence time of the impact process. The authors identify a new droplet bouncing mode, termed the 'bouncing-with-spray' (BWS) mode, which significantly reduces residence time compared to the traditional 'retraction-bouncing' (RB) mode. The BWS mode is induced by the burst of vapor bubbles within the liquid film, which creates holes in the film and causes the liquid to recoil from these holes, thereby shortening the recoiling distance and time. The study demonstrates that this heat-induced approach is simple, reliable, and avoids the surface degradation associated with microstructured surfaces. Experimental results show that the residence time in the BWS mode is independent of liquid viscosity. A theoretical model is proposed based on energy balance and a critical condition where the vapor bubble radius equals the minimum film thickness. This model yields a scaling law for the transition boundary between RB and BWS modes in the film boiling regime, expressed as ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ for constant liquid and droplet size. The scaling law agrees well with experimental data and also explains the transition behavior in the transition boiling regime. The findings provide physical insight into impact dynamics and offer a practical method for optimizing processes requiring rapid droplet departure, such as anti-icing and self-cleaning.

Research Context
Droplet impact is ubiquitous in industrial applications like spray cooling and inkjet printing. Previous studies focused on impact morphologies and ejected secondary droplets. The Leidenfrost effect creates a vapor layer that insulates the droplet. Reducing contact time is crucial for anti-icing and self-cleaning applications. Existing strategies involve complex surface microstructures or modifications.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to identify a mode that reduces droplet residence time. The authors hypothesize that heat-induced bubble bursting can shorten residence time. The BWS mode is predicted to have a shorter residence time than RB mode. A scaling law is proposed for the transition between bouncing modes. The model is expected to explain transitions in both film and transition boiling.

Methodological Details
The experiment used water, ethanol, and water/glycerol mixtures. Droplets were generated by a syringe pump at low speed. The substrate was a polished silicon wafer heated by a copper holder. Temperature was controlled with an accuracy of ±1°C using a PID controller. High-speed cameras captured side-view and aerial-view images of the impact. Droplet sizes varied from 1.6 mm to 3.4 mm depending on the liquid. Impact speeds ranged from 0.9 to 2.1 m/s. Weber numbers were varied from 10 to 180. Viscosity was varied by changing glycerol concentration in water mixtures.

Procedures And Architectures
The theoretical model assumes the vapor layer has uniform thickness. Heat transfer in the vapor layer is dominated by conduction. The critical condition is when the bubble radius equals the minimum film thickness. The time interval for heat transfer is approximated by the maximum expansion time. The minimum film thickness scales with Reynolds number to the power of -2/5. The maximum expansion diameter scales with Weber number to the power of 0.35. The average heat transfer coefficient is derived from vapor layer physics. The transition boundary is derived by substituting these relations into the energy balance.

Key Results
The residence time in BWS mode is significantly smaller than in RB mode. In the film boiling regime, BWS mode residence time is also reduced. The dimensionless residence time for RB mode is approximately 2.3. The dimensionless residence time for BWS mode is approximately 1.4. The residence time reduction in BWS mode is about 40%. The residence time in BWS mode is independent of liquid viscosity. The scaling law ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ agrees well with experimental data. The transition temperature increases with Weber number in transition boiling.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The reduction in residence time is due to the burst of vapor bubbles. Bubble bursting creates holes in the liquid film. The liquid film recoils from these holes, shortening the recoiling distance. This mechanism is similar to droplet fragmentation on ridged surfaces. The heat-induced approach is reliable and avoids surface degradation. The model provides physical insight into impact dynamics.

Contradictions And Limitations
The model assumes a uniform vapor layer thickness. The heat transfer area is assumed constant for different liquids. The study does not provide detailed numerical simulations of bubble bursting. The scaling exponent n may vary for different surface structures.

Claims
The bouncing-with-spray mode significantly reduces droplet residence time compared to the retraction-bouncing mode. Experimental data shows residence time of 6.5 ms vs 12.0 ms. Dimensionless residence time is 1.4 vs 2.3. The reduction is dependent on the boiling regime and impact parameters. 
The transition between bouncing modes follows a scaling law of ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ in the film boiling regime. Experimental data agrees well with the proposed scaling law. The scaling law is derived from energy balance and critical conditions. The scaling exponent may vary with surface structure. 

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study varied viscosity to test its effect on residence time. The residence time was found to be independent of viscosity. The scaling law was tested against experimental data in the film boiling regime.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the schematic of the experimental setup. Figure 2 shows impact morphologies in three boiling regimes. Figure 3 shows the burst of vapor bubbles in the BWS mode. Figure 4 shows the effect of viscosity on residence time. Figure 5 compares dimensionless residence time for RB and BWS modes. Figure 6 shows the theoretical model and regime map. Table 1 summarizes the properties of the liquids used.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of the bouncing-with-spray mode that reduces residence time. 2. The strongest evidence is the 40% reduction in residence time and the agreement of the scaling law with data. 3. The future path involves detailed numerical simulations and experimental measurements of bubble bursting.
